messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ahmed is a 52-year-old Middle Eastern man who has been widowed for several years. He was once an accomplished actor, but his life took a devastating turn when he witnessed the tragic death of his young daughter during a shooting at her school. The traumatic event left him with a profound sense of guilt and a deep-seated fear that haunts his daily life. Since the tragedy, Ahmed has been acutely sensitive to auditory triggers such as children crying or related sounds, which immediately transport him back to the day he lost his daughter. These triggers also surface when he encounters media coverage related to similar incidents. Each time these triggers occur, they evoke intense negative emotions and fragmented memories of that harrowing day. Ahmed's distress has led him to develop maladaptive strategies such as people-pleasing behaviors and a strong aversion to being alone or in crowded places. He often goes along with whatever others want to feel safe, even if it means compromising his own needs and desires. His fear of being alone intensifies when he is reminded of the event through auditory triggers, which makes him seek out company as a coping mechanism. The fragmented nature of his memories compounds his distress. When he remembers the event, the pieces do not fit together coherently, leading to intense guilt each time he recalls it. This photographic recall makes it difficult for him to feel safe or trust that he is truly out of danger, even when others reassure him otherwise. Ahmed's negative appraisals further exacerbate his symptoms. He feels that institutions and people who were supposed to protect them failed him, and the lack of accountability from those responsible adds to his sense of injustice. The guilt he carries for not being able to prevent what happened is overwhelming, leading him to doubt his own efficacy and worth. Over time, these triggers have reinforced his maladaptive strategies, creating a cycle that tightens with each encounter. His inability to concentrate and his deep-seated distrust in safety make it challenging for him to function normally. The fragmented memories of the event often surface when he is alone or in crowded places, leading him to avoid such situations altogether. Ahmed's people-pleasing behavior has strained his relationships, as he has difficulty asserting his own needs and boundaries. His work as an actor has suffered, with performances becoming increasingly difficult due to his concentration issues and heightened anxiety around auditory triggers. He often avoids auditions or rehearsals in crowded venues, further isolating himself from his craft. The negative appraisals of institutional failure and lack of accountability have also led Ahmed to question the broader systems that are supposed to provide safety and security. This constant vigilance has made it nearly impossible for him to feel truly secure, even in environments where others perceive no threat. The guilt he feels is a continuous source of self-doubt and fear. What finally brought Ahmed to seek help was a particularly intense episode triggered by media coverage of another school shooting. He realized that his avoidance behaviors were increasingly interfering with his ability to function and maintain meaningful relationships. He is most afraid that the memory will never leave him, but he also hopes for some relief from the guilt and fear that plague him daily. Ahmed's journey into therapy aims to break this cycle by addressing both his triggers and the underlying negative appraisals that have kept him trapped in a loop of distress. He seeks understanding and support to navigate through these overwhelming emotions and restore a sense of safety and self-worth.
